title: How to Declutter Before the Holiday Gifts Arrive (A Gentle November Plan)
description: New stuff is coming in December. Make room now with a low-energy November declutter plan for toys, kitchen gadgets, clothes and the hall closet.
intro:
Every January, the same thing happens. New gifts come in, nothing goes out, and the house that felt full in November now feels like it's closing in on us.

The new stuff isn't the problem. The problem is that there's no empty space waiting for it. So it lands on the floor, the counter or the "I'll deal with it later" pile, and later never comes.

November is the sweet spot. The holidays are close enough to feel real, but the chaos hasn't started yet. Here's a gentle plan to make room before the boxes show up, in small jobs you can do on a tired weeknight.

sections.heading: Start with the question, not the closet
sections.body:
Before you open a single drawer, think about what's coming in. Kids getting new toys? You getting a kitchen gadget? Clothes from Grandma?

Write a quick list of the **categories** of stuff you expect. That list tells you exactly where to make room. No need to declutter the whole house. Only the spots where new things will land.

sections.heading: Use the 'one bag a day' rule
sections.body:
Huge declutter weekends tend to end with every drawer dumped on the bed and zero energy left. Try one bag a day instead.

Grab a grocery bag. Set a 10-minute timer. Fill it with things to donate or toss. When the timer rings, the bag goes straight to the car. Thirty small bags by December is a lot of space, and you never had to face one giant mess.

sections.heading: Toys: let kids help (a little)
sections.body:
Kids often let go of toys more easily when there's something exciting coming. Try a simple pitch: "Let's make room for new things. Pick five toys another kid would love."

A few tips that make it go smoother:

- Keep it short. 10 minutes, then stop.
- Skip the giant toy bin dump. Pull out one shelf or one basket at a time.
- Broken toys and pieces of sets with missing parts can go without a vote.
- Bag donations right away and get them out of sight so they don't get re-adopted.

sections.heading: Kitchen: clear one cabinet
sections.body:
If a new gadget or dishes might be coming, empty one cabinet now. Pull out anything you haven't used since last winter: the second salad spinner, the mugs with chips, the novelty pan you used once.

You don't need to reorganize the whole kitchen. One clear shelf ready for something new is the goal.

sections.heading: Clothes: the hanger trick
sections.body:
Turn every hanger in your closet backward. When you wear something, hang it back the normal way. By late December, you'll see what you actually reach for.

For now, pull anything that doesn't fit, needs a repair you'll never make, or makes you feel bad. Those can go now and free up space for anything cozy that comes your way.

sections.heading: Make a 'where will it live?' list
sections.body:
Here's a small trick that saves January. On your gift list, next to each big gift, write where it will live. The new art kit goes in the craft drawer. The air fryer goes where the toaster oven was.

If you can't think of a spot, that's your sign to either make room now or pick a gift that takes less space. Experiences, consumables and gift cards are great clutter-free options.

sections.heading: Get donations out of the house
sections.body:
The sneaky part of decluttering: the donation bag that sits by the door for three months. Pick a donation day on the calendar every week in November. Put the bags in the car the night before. Drop them on your way somewhere you already go.

Out of the house is the finish line. A bag in the trunk counts as progress, too.

sections.heading: If you only do one thing
sections.body: Clear the spot where gifts get unwrapped. Usually that's the living room. Pick up the floor, clear one shelf and empty one basket. On the big day, wrapping paper goes in a trash bag, new things go in the empty basket, and the room doesn't explode.

outro:
Decluttering before the holidays isn't about owning less for the sake of it. It's about giving new things a place to land so January feels lighter, not heavier.

If a printed plan helps you stick with it, the *Tidy Brain Printable Pack* has declutter checklists you can tape to the fridge and check off one bag at a time.
